{{Short description|Local bifurcation in which two fixed points of a dynamical system collide and anni}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] area of [[bifurcation theory]] a '''saddle-node bifurcation''', '''tangential bifurcation''' or '''fold bifurcation''' is a [[local bifurcation]] in which two [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]s (or [[equilibrium point|equilibria]]) of a [[dynamical system]] collide and annihilate each other. The term 'saddle-node bifurcation' is most often used in reference to continuous dynamical systems. In discrete dynamical systems, the same bifurcation is often instead called a '''fold bifurcation'''.  Another name is '''blue sky bifurcation''' in reference to the sudden creation of two fixed points.{{sfn|Strogatz|1994|p=47}}

If the phase space is one-dimensional, one of the equilibrium points is unstable (the saddle), while the other is stable (the node).

Saddle-node bifurcations may be associated with [[hysteresis|hysteresis loops]] and [[catastrophe theory|catastrophes]].

==Normal form==

A typical example of a differential equation with a saddle-node bifurcation is:

:<math>\frac{dx}{dt}=r+x^2.</math>

Here <math>x</math> is the state variable and <math>r</math> is the bifurcation parameter.
*If <math>r<0</math> there are two equilibrium points, a stable equilibrium point at <math>-\sqrt{-r}</math> and an unstable one at <math>+\sqrt{-r}</math>.
*At <math>r=0</math> (the bifurcation point) there is exactly one equilibrium point. At this point the fixed point is no longer [[Hyperbolic equilibrium point|hyperbolic]]. In this case the fixed point is called a saddle-node fixed point.
*If <math>r>0</math> there are no equilibrium points.{{sfn|Kuznetsov|1998|pp=80–81}}

[[File:Fold Bifurcation.webm|thumb|Saddle node bifurcation]]

In fact, this is a [[normal form (bifurcation theory)|normal form]] of a saddle-node bifurcation. A scalar differential equation <math> \tfrac{dx}{dt} = f(r,x) </math> which has a fixed point at <math> x = 0 </math> for <math> r = 0 </math> with <math> \tfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) = 0 </math> is locally [[topological conjugacy|topologically equivalent]] to <math> \frac{dx}{dt} = r \pm x^2 </math>, provided it satisfies <math> \tfrac{\partial^2\! f}{\partial x^2}(0,0) \ne 0 </math> and <math> \tfrac{\partial f}{\partial r}(0,0) \ne 0 </math>. The first condition is the nondegeneracy condition and the second condition is the transversality condition.{{sfn|Kuznetsov|1998|loc=Theorems 3.1 and 3.2}}

==Example in two dimensions==
[[Image:Saddlenode.gif|thumb|right|300px|Phase portrait showing saddle-node bifurcation]]
An example of a saddle-node bifurcation in two dimensions occurs in the two-dimensional dynamical system:

:<math> \frac {dx} {dt} = \alpha - x^2 </math>
:<math> \frac {dy} {dt} = - y.</math>

As can be seen by the animation obtained by plotting phase portraits by varying the parameter <math> \alpha </math>,
* When <math> \alpha </math> is negative, there are no equilibrium points.
* When <math> \alpha = 0</math>, there is a saddle-node point.
* When <math> \alpha </math> is positive, there are two equilibrium points: that is, one [[saddle point]] and one node (either an attractor or a repellor).

Other examples are in modelling biological switches.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Chong |first1=Ket Hing |last2=Samarasinghe |first2=Sandhya|author2-link=Sandhya Samarasinghe |last3=Kulasiri |first3=Don |last4=Zheng |first4=Jie |year=2015 |title=Computational techniques in mathematical modelling of biological switches |conference=21st International Congress on Modelling and Simulation |hdl=10220/42793 }}</ref> Recently, it was shown that under certain conditions, the Einstein field equations of General Relativity have the same form as a fold bifurcation.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.geomphys.2017.10.001 |title=Einstein's field equations as a fold bifurcation |journal=Journal of Geometry and Physics |volume=123 |pages=434–7 |year=2018 |last1=Kohli |first1=Ikjyot Singh |last2=Haslam |first2=Michael C |arxiv=1607.05300 |bibcode=2018JGP...123..434K |s2cid=119196982 }}</ref> A non-autonomous version of the saddle-node bifurcation (i.e. the parameter is time-dependent) has also been studied.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=Jeremiah H.|last2=Ye|first2=Felix X. -F.|last3=Qian|first3=Hong|last4=Huang|first4=Sui|date=2019-08-01|title=Time-dependent saddle–node bifurcation: Breaking time and the point of no return in a non-autonomous model of critical transitions|journal=Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena|volume=395|pages=7–14|doi=10.1016/j.physd.2019.02.005|pmid=31700198 |pmc=6836434 |issn=0167-2789|arxiv=1611.09542|bibcode=2019PhyD..395....7L }}</ref>
